title: The Puzzling Gap In Research On Writing Instruction
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler argues that research on writing instruction is thin and has overlooked a basic question: whether novice writers should learn to write sentences well before being asked to write at length. She grounds the case in working memory, since composing taxes the mind with spelling, word choice, structure and ideas all at once. She surveys what is known (process approaches, SRSD, the Writers Workshop evaluation) and notes that no approach is clearly superior and that multi-component programs are hard to untangle. Her move is to propose that sentence-level, content-grounded activities such as fragment completion and sentence combining may free up working memory while building knowledge. She uses The Writing Revolution as her example and discloses that she co-authored its book and sits on its advisory board.
points: Writing is harder than reading and far less studied, with only about a quarter of students proficient on national writing tests.
Existing research shows several approaches work in some studies and fail in others, so no method has been shown clearly superior.
The untested hypothesis is that starting at the sentence level reduces working-memory load and so makes room for conventions and content.
Sentence activities grounded in curriculum content, such as turning fragments into complete sentences, build knowledge as well as mechanics.
Wexler openly discloses her ties to The Writing Revolution, which tempers but does not remove the force of her call for research.
quotes: Writing may be the hardest thing we ask students to do in school. Studies have shown that writing places a huge burden on “working memory,” a term used to describe what happens in the mind when it processes information.
Writing is much harder than reading—difficult as that is. On national writing tests, only about a quarter of students score proficient or above.

To be fair, it’s hard to conduct a study that points to a clear causal relationship between a particular method of instruction and a better outcome. The kind of research allowing for that—a randomized controlled trial—requires identifying two large and similar groups of students, only one of which is exposed to the method, and following them while trying to control for confounding factors (like teachers who deviate from the method).
Still, there’s a puzzling gap in writing research: examining whether it’s best to start instruction at the sentence level. There are reasons to suspect that approach would help:

That’s true, but one kind of sentence-level activity, sentence combining, has been shown to produce good results. Instead of just learning rules, students take several short sentences and combine them into one longer, more complex sentence.

Studies have found that teaching grammar in the abstract isn’t effective, but teaching grammar in the context of students’ own writing is—and it’s a lot easier to do that at the sentence level than in the context of pages of error-filled writing.

We don’t yet have studies of the impact of an approach that, like The Writing Revolution, starts with knowledge-building sentence-level activities. Given our general lack of progress in improving students’ writing, maybe it’s time we did.
